'''''Albizia lebbeck''''' is a species of plant in the family [[Fabaceae]], native to the Indian subcontinent and [[Myanmar]].<ref name=IUCN/><ref>Lowry, J.B. & Seebeck, J. 1997 "The Potential for Tropical Agroforestry in Wood and Animal Feed Production". Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation, Indooroopilly, Queensland</ref> It is widely cultivated and [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in other [[tropical]] and [[subtropical]] regions, including Australia. Common names in English include '''siris''', '''Indian siris''', '''East Indian walnut''', '''Broome raintree''', '''lebbeck''', '''lebbek tree''', '''frywood''', '''koko''' and '''woman's tongue tree'''.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 9 March 2023}}</ref> The latter name is a play on the sound the seeds make as they rattle inside the pods. '''Siris''' is also a common name of the genus ''[[Albizia]]''.

==Description==
It is a [[tree]] growing to a height of {{cvt|18|–|30|m}} tall with a trunk {{cvt|.5|to|1|m}} in diameter. The [[leaf|leaves]] are bipinnate, {{cvt|7.5|–|15|cm|0}} long, with one to four pairs of pinnae, each pinna with 6–18 leaflets. The [[flower]]s are white, with numerous {{cvt|2.5|–|3.8|cm|1}} long stamens, and very fragrant. The [[fruit]] is a [[legume|pod]] {{cvt|15|–|30|cm|0}} long and {{cvt|2.5|-|5.0|cm|0}} broad, containing six to twelve [[seed]]s.<ref>Ali (1973)</ref>

== Habitat ==
''Albizia lebbeck'' is found in a wide range of climates ranging from semi-desert, to humid regions.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Rojas-Sandoval, Datiles, Acevedo-Rodriguez |date=2022 |title=Albizia lebbeck (Indian siris) |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.4008 |journal=Cabi Compendium|volume=CABI Compendium |page=4008 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.4008 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It can endure long cold winters, as well as very dry climate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kehlenbeck |first1=Katja |last2=Kindt |first2=Roeland |last3=Sinclair |first3=Fergus L. |last4=Simons |first4=Anthony J. |last5=Jamnadass |first5=Ramni |date=2011-08-18 |title=Exotic tree species displace indigenous ones on farms at intermediate altitudes around Mount Kenya |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=83 |issue=2 |pages=133–147 |doi=10.1007/s10457-011-9413-4 |bibcode=2011AgrSy..83..133K |issn=0167-4366}}</ref> ''A. lebbeck'' is a drought-tolerant tree that can be found throughout the tropics. Due to its ability to adapt to a broad spectrum of climates, this species has spread to different tropical regions throughout the world as an invasive species.<ref>{{Cite web |last=London |title=Albizia lebbeck (L.) Benth. |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000184271 |website=The World Flora Online}}</ref>

==Name==
'''''Mimosa speciosa''''' as described by [[Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin]] refers to ''Albizia lebbeck''. ''Mimosa speciosa'' of [[Carl Peter Thunberg]], however, is ''[[Albizia julibrissin]]''. The species epithet 'lebbeck' is derived from the Arabic word (لَبَّخ).<ref name=":1" />

Albizia is named after [[Francesco Albizzi]], an Italian naturalist. It is also commonly referred to as siris, its Hindi name.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parrotta |first=John |date=2014 |title=Albizia Lebbek |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/288327955 |website=ResearchGate}}</ref>

In the [[West Indies]] and certain parts of [[South America]] this tree is known as a 'Shak Shak Tree' because of the sound the seeds make in the pod.{{cn|date=September 2025}}

== Uses ==
Its uses include environmental management, [[Fodder|forage]], medicine and wood.  It is cultivated as a shade tree in [[North America|North]] and [[South America]].<ref name = ildis>ILDIS (2005)</ref> In India and Pakistan, the tree is used to produce [[timber]]. Wood from ''Albizia lebbeck'' has a density of 0.55-0.66 g/cm<sup>3</sup> or higher.<ref>Brown (1997)</ref>

[[Image:Bark of Albizia lebbeck.jpg|thumb|left|150px|Bark on a tree in Hong Kong]]
Even where it is not native, some indigenous [[herbivore]]s are liable to utilize lebbeck as a food resource. For example, the [[greater rhea]] (''Rhea americana'') has been observed feeding on it in the [[cerrado]] of [[Brazil]].<ref>Schetini de Azevedo ''et al.'' (2006)</ref>

===Ethnobotany===
Lebbeck is an [[astringent]], also used by some cultures to treat boils, [[cough]], to treat the [[human eye|eye]], [[flu]], [[gingivitis]], [[human lung|lung]] problems, pectoral problems, is used as a tonic, and is used to treat abdominal [[tumor]]s.<ref>Duke (2008)</ref> The bark is used medicinally to treat [[inflammation]].<ref>Lowry ''et al.''(1994)</ref> This information was obtained via [[ethnobotany|ethnobotanical records]], which are a reference to how a plant is used by indigenous peoples, not verifiable, scientific or medical evaluation of the effectiveness of these claims. ''Albizia lebbeck'' is also [[psychoactive]]. It is also very effective in migraine. All parts of the plant are useful, such as the leaves, root, and stem.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Balkrishna, Sakshi, Chauhan, Dabas, Arya |date=22 March 2022 |title=A Comprehensive Insight into the Phytochemical, Pharmacological Potential, and Traditional Medicinal Uses of Albizia lebbeck (L.) Benth. |journal=Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1155/2022/5359669 |doi-access=free |pmid=35497931 |pmc=9050289 }}</ref> The flowers of the plant are traditionally used in Chinese traditional medicine to treat [[insomnia]].<ref name=":0" />

==Taxonomy==
The [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] history of ''A. lebbeck'' is somewhat convoluted. It was originally described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] as ''Mimosa lebbeck''. In its original description the ''Mimosa lebbeck'' was a large Acacia tree that grew in Egypt.<ref>Book: [https://books.google.com/books?id=LkIGAAAAQAAJ&q=mimosa%20lebbeck ''Voyages and Travels in the Levant in the Years 1749, 50, 51, 52, Containing Observations in Natural History''], by Fredrik Hasselquist (died 1752), written originally in the Swedish language, published in 1757 by Carl Linnaeus (died 1778), published in English translation in 1766. It says ''Mimosa Lebbeck'' is a large Acacia tree of southern Egypt and is grown in northern Egypt in gardens. This botany item was also copied by Linnaeus into Linnaeus's own botany book.</ref> [[George Bentham]] placed the [[species]] in its present [[genus]], but other authors believed that the plant described by Linnaeus was the related ''[[Albizia kalkora]]'' as described by Prain (based on the ''Mimosa kalkora'' of [[William Roxburgh]]), and erroneously referred to this species as ''Albizia lebbeck''. However, [[Francisco Manuel Blanco]] used ''Mimosa lebbeck'' to refer to ''[[Albizia retusa]]'' ssp. ''retusa''. In addition, the [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] is occasionally misspelled ''lebbek''.<ref>USDA (1994), ILDIS (2005)</ref>

[[Junior synonym]]s are:<ref name = ildis />
* ''Acacia lebbeck'' <small>(L.) [[Willd.]]</small>
* ''Acacia macrophylla'' <small>[[Alexander G. von Bunge|Bunge]]</small>
* ''Acacia speciosa'' <small>(Jacq.) Willd.</small>
* ''Albizia latifolia'' <small>B.Boivin</small>
* ''Albizia lebbeck'' <small>(L.) Benth.</small> var. ''leucoxylon'' <small>Hassk.</small>
* ''Albizia lebbeck'' <small>(L.) Benth.</small> var. ''pubescens'' <small>Haines</small>
* ''Albizia lebbeck'' <small>(L.) Benth.</small> var. ''rostrata'' <small>Haines</small>
:''Albizia rostrata'' <small>Miq.</small> is ''[[Archidendron globosum]]''.
* ''Feuilleea lebbeck'' <small>(L.) [[Otto Kuntze|Kuntze]]</small>
* ''Inga borbonica'' <small>Hassk.</small>
* ''Inga leucoxylon'' <small>Hassk.</small>
* ''Mimosa lebbeck'' <small>L.</small>
* ''Mimosa lebbek'' <small>L. (orth.var.)</small>
* ''Mimosa sirissa'' <small>Roxb.</small>
* ''Mimosa speciosa'' <small>[[Jacq.]]</small>
:''Mimosa speciosa'' <small>Thunb.</small> is ''[[Albizia julibrissin]]''.
* ''Pithecellobium splitgerberianum'' <small>[[Miq.]]</small>

Independently, there also exists a genus named ''[[Lebeckia]]'', whose range is restricted to South Africa. It is also a legume, but a member of the [[Faboideae]], a different legume [[subfamily]].
